dx: Langerhans cell histiocytosis with lytic skull lesions and central diabetes insipidus
case: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of increased thirst and urination for 2 months and a painless swelling on his head. He wakes at night to drink water. His temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 96/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a 2-cm soft, nontender mass over the left parietal bone and a scaly papular eruption on the scalp. Serum sodium is 147 mEq/L (reference, 135 to 145 mEq/L), and serum osmolality is 302 mOsm/kg H2O (reference, 275 to 295 mOsm/kg H2O). Urine osmolality is 110 mOsm/kg H2O and rises after desmopressin is given. X-rays show several punched-out lytic lesions of the skull. Biopsy of the mass shows sheets of histiocytes with grooved nuclei and many eosinophils. Diagnosis: Langerhans cell histiocytosis with central diabetes insipidus.

questions.stem: Immunohistochemical staining shows that the lesional histiocytes are positive for CD1a and S100. Electron microscopy of these cells is most likely to show which of the following?
options: Auer rods
Russell bodies
Birbeck granules
Weibel-Palade bodies
approach: CD1a and S100 positivity identify the lesional cells as Langerhans cells.
Langerhans cells contain a unique cytoplasmic organelle seen by electron microscopy.
That organelle is the rod-shaped Birbeck granule, which can have a terminal bulge like a tennis racket.
questions.why: Langerhans cell histiocytosis is a clonal proliferation of Langerhans-type dendritic cells. These cells are CD1a positive and S100 positive (and langerin, CD207, positive). On electron microscopy they contain Birbeck granules, rod-shaped organelles that sometimes have a bulb at one end. Children present with lytic bone lesions (eosinophilic granuloma when single) or with multisystem disease, in which pituitary stalk involvement causes central diabetes insipidus.
whyNot: Auer rods are fused azurophilic granules in myeloblasts of acute myeloid leukemia.
Russell bodies are cytoplasmic inclusions of stored immunoglobulin in plasma cells.
Correct.
Weibel-Palade bodies store von Willebrand factor and P-selectin in endothelial cells.

questions.stem: The many eosinophils in the lesion are recruited from the blood. These eosinophils developed in the bone marrow from which of the following progenitor cells?
options: Common myeloid progenitor
Common lymphoid progenitor
Megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitor
Early thymic T cell progenitor
approach: Start at the hematopoietic stem cell, which splits into common myeloid and common lymphoid progenitors.
The lymphoid branch makes B cells, T cells, and NK cells.
The myeloid branch makes granulocytes (including eosinophils), monocytes, red cells, and megakaryocytes.
questions.why: All blood cells come from the hematopoietic stem cell. It gives rise to a common myeloid progenitor and a common lymphoid progenitor. The common myeloid progenitor gives rise to the granulocyte and monocyte lines (neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes) and to the megakaryocyte-erythroid line. Eosinophil production is driven mainly by IL-5. The common lymphoid progenitor gives rise to B cells, T cells, and NK cells.
whyNot: Correct.
The common lymphoid progenitor makes B cells, T cells, and NK cells. It does not make granulocytes.
The megakaryocyte-erythroid progenitor branches off the myeloid line and makes only red cells and platelets.
Early thymic progenitors give rise to T cells in the thymus, not to granulocytes.

questions.stem: Before the biopsy, the differential diagnosis of the skull lesion included acute bacterial osteomyelitis. Which of the following findings on a complete blood count would most support a pyogenic bacterial infection?
options: Eosinophilia
Basophilia
Lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes
Neutrophilia with increased band forms
approach: Pyogenic bacteria are cleared mainly by neutrophils, which phagocytose and kill them.
Bacterial infection triggers release of neutrophils, including immature band forms, from the marrow reserve.
So neutrophilia with a left shift points to bacterial infection.
questions.why: Each white cell type has a typical trigger. Neutrophils are the first-line phagocytes against bacteria, and acute bacterial infection releases mature and band neutrophils from the marrow (a left shift). Eosinophilia points to parasitic (especially tissue helminth) or allergic disease. Lymphocytosis, often with atypical reactive lymphocytes, points to viral infection. Basophilia is uncommon and suggests a myeloproliferative neoplasm such as CML.
whyNot: Eosinophilia suggests helminth infection or allergic disease. It does not suggest a pyogenic bacterial infection.
Basophilia is rare in infection and is a clue to chronic myeloid leukemia or another myeloproliferative neoplasm.
Lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes is typical of viral infection such as infectious mononucleosis.
Correct.

questions.stem: During chemotherapy for multisystem disease, the boy receives a unit of packed red cells. Within 15 minutes he develops fever, flank pain, hypotension, and red urine. A clerical error is found; group A blood was given to a group O recipient. This reaction belongs to the same hypersensitivity type as which of the following?
options: Anaphylaxis in IgA deficiency
Hemolytic disease of the newborn
Mixed cryoglobulinemic vasculitis
Allergic contact dermatitis
approach: Recognize an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction from ABO-incompatible blood.
Preformed recipient anti-A antibodies bind donor red cell antigens and fix complement, which is type II hypersensitivity.
Find the other condition caused by antibodies against a cell-surface antigen.
questions.why: In an ABO-incompatible transfusion, the recipient's preformed IgM anti-A antibodies bind the donor red cells and activate complement, causing intravascular hemolysis within minutes. Antibody directed against an antigen on a cell surface is type II hypersensitivity. Hemolytic disease of the newborn is also type II: maternal IgG crosses the placenta and coats fetal red cells, which are then destroyed. Autoimmune hemolytic anemia belongs here too.
whyNot: Anaphylaxis to IgA in an IgA-deficient recipient is type I hypersensitivity, mediated by IgE on mast cells.
Correct.
Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis is type III. Circulating immune complexes deposit in vessel walls and activate complement.
Allergic contact dermatitis is type IV, a delayed reaction mediated by sensitized T cells.

dx: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with thrombosis after pancreaticoduodenectomy
case: A 63-year-old woman undergoes pancreaticoduodenectomy for adenocarcinoma of the head of the pancreas. Subcutaneous unfractionated heparin is started on the first postoperative day for thromboprophylaxis. Her platelet count is 260,000/mm3 (reference, 150,000 to 400,000/mm3) before surgery and 95,000/mm3 on postoperative day 7. On day 8 she develops swelling and pain of the left calf. Her temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 128/76 mm Hg. Duplex ultrasonography shows thrombus in the left femoral and popliteal veins. An immunoassay for antibodies against platelet factor 4 and heparin is positive, and a serotonin release assay is positive. Diagnosis: heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with thrombosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following mechanisms best explains both the fall in her platelet count and her venous thrombosis?
options: IgG against PF4-heparin complexes activating platelets
IgG against platelet GpIIb/IIIa causing splenic clearance
Direct nonimmune aggregation of platelets by heparin
Loss of ADAMTS13 activity leaving large vWF multimers
approach: A platelet drop of more than half, 5 to 10 days after starting heparin, with new thrombosis is the classic pattern.
The positive PF4-heparin immunoassay and serotonin release assay show a functional, platelet-activating antibody.
Activated platelets aggregate and release procoagulant microparticles, so platelets fall while clots form.
questions.why: Heparin binds platelet factor 4 (PF4), a positively charged protein released from platelet granules, and the complex exposes new epitopes. The patient makes IgG against PF4-heparin. These immune complexes bind platelet Fc gamma receptors (FcγRIIa) and activate the platelets, which aggregate, release more PF4, and generate thrombin. Activated platelets are cleared, so the count falls, and the same activation produces venous and arterial thrombosis. This is why HIT is a prothrombotic disorder even though platelets are low.
whyNot: Correct.
Antibodies against GpIIb/IIIa cause immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), which causes bleeding, not thrombosis.
Nonimmune heparin-associated thrombocytopenia occurs in the first 1 to 2 days, is mild, and does not cause thrombosis.
ADAMTS13 deficiency causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, with schistocytes and microvascular platelet thrombi rather than large-vein thrombosis.

questions.stem: Five months before her cancer was diagnosed, she had several episodes of tender, cordlike superficial veins that appeared in the right forearm, resolved, and then appeared in the left thigh. Which of the following most likely explains those episodes?
options: Ectopic erythropoietin raising red cell mass
Inherited factor V resistant to activated protein C
Procoagulant mucins and tissue factor from tumor
Immune complex deposition in small-vessel walls
approach: Recurrent superficial venous thrombosis that moves from site to site is migratory thrombophlebitis.
Appearing before a pancreatic adenocarcinoma is found, it is a paraneoplastic syndrome (Trousseau syndrome).
The tumor releases procoagulants such as mucin and tissue factor that activate coagulation.
questions.why: Trousseau syndrome is migratory thrombophlebitis linked to an underlying cancer, classically mucin-secreting adenocarcinoma of the pancreas, stomach, or lung. Tumor cells release tissue factor, mucins, and other procoagulants that activate coagulation throughout the body. The thromboses can appear before the cancer is found, so unexplained migratory thrombophlebitis calls for a search for malignancy. Other hematologic paraneoplastic syndromes include erythrocytosis from ectopic erythropoietin (renal cell and hepatocellular carcinoma) and pure red cell aplasia with thymoma.
whyNot: Ectopic erythropoietin from renal cell or hepatocellular carcinoma causes erythrocytosis, not migratory superficial thrombophlebitis.
Factor V Leiden raises lifelong risk of deep venous thrombosis but does not cause migratory superficial thrombophlebitis heralding a cancer.
Correct.
Immune complex deposition in small vessels causes leukocytoclastic vasculitis with palpable purpura, not tender cordlike veins that move from site to site.

questions.stem: After heparin is stopped, her platelet count recovers. She then begins adjuvant chemotherapy. Assuming a single cycle abruptly halts marrow output and there is no bleeding or hemolysis, which of the following patterns of blood counts is expected over the next 3 weeks?
options: Anemia first, then neutropenia, then thrombocytopenia
Neutropenia and thrombocytopenia first, anemia much later
Anemia and thrombocytopenia first, neutropenia much later
Thrombocytopenia first, then anemia, then neutropenia
approach: When production stops, a cell count falls at a rate set by how long that cell survives in the blood.
Neutrophils circulate for only hours, and platelets live about 7 to 10 days.
Red cells live about 120 days, so hemoglobin falls only about 1% per day and anemia appears last.
questions.why: After sudden marrow suppression, the cells with the shortest life span disappear first. Neutrophils circulate for less than a day, so neutropenia follows as soon as the marrow reserve is used up, usually within 1 to 2 weeks. Platelets survive about 7 to 10 days, so thrombocytopenia appears on a similar time scale. Red cells survive about 120 days, so loss of production lowers hemoglobin slowly, and anemia comes much later unless there is bleeding or hemolysis.
whyNot: Anemia cannot come first after marrow suppression, because red cells have the longest life span (about 120 days).
Correct.
Red cells outlive neutrophils by months, so anemia does not appear with or before neutropenia.
Thrombocytopenia does appear early, but neutropenia appears at least as early and anemia comes last, not in the middle.

questions.stem: Even without heparin, she was at high risk for deep venous thrombosis. Postoperative bed rest contributes to that risk mainly through which of the following?
options: Injury of venous endothelium exposing tissue factor
Antibody-mediated activation of circulating platelets
Increased hepatic production of procoagulant proteins
Loss of calf muscle pump action, slowing venous flow
approach: Virchow triad: stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability.
Immobility removes the calf muscle pump, so blood pools in deep leg veins.
Stasis keeps activated clotting factors in place and lets platelets reach the vessel wall.
questions.why: Virchow triad names three conditions that promote thrombosis: stasis of blood, injury to the endothelium, and hypercoagulability. Bed rest abolishes the calf muscle pump, so flow in deep leg veins slows. Slow flow prevents dilution and clearance of activated clotting factors and lets platelets contact the endothelium. In this patient, surgery adds endothelial injury and a hypercoagulable state, and her pancreatic adenocarcinoma adds hypercoagulability. Pregnancy and estrogen use act mainly by raising clotting factor levels.
whyNot: Endothelial injury is the surgery's contribution, not the contribution of immobility.
Antibody-mediated platelet activation is the mechanism of HIT, which is separate from the risk created by bed rest.
Higher hepatic production of clotting factors is how estrogen and pregnancy cause hypercoagulability.
Correct.

dx: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia with warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia (Evans syndrome)
case: A 71-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue and easy bruising for 3 weeks. His temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 132/78 mm Hg. He has scleral icterus, petechiae on the legs, painless cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy, and a spleen tip palpable 3 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL (reference, 13.5 to 17.5 g/dL), reticulocytes 9% (reference, 0.5% to 2.5%), platelets 18,000/mm3 (reference, 150,000 to 400,000/mm3), and leukocytes 62,000/mm3 (reference, 4,500 to 11,000/mm3) with 85% small mature lymphocytes and many smudge cells. Serum LDH is 480 U/L (reference, 140 to 280 U/L), and haptoglobin is undetectable. Flow cytometry shows a clonal B cell population positive for CD5 and CD23. Diagnosis: chronic lymphocytic leukemia with autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: During the past 2 years he has had three episodes of pneumococcal pneumonia. His absolute neutrophil count is 2,800/mm3 (reference, 1,500 to 8,000/mm3). Which of the following best explains his susceptibility to these infections?
options: Deficiency of terminal complement components
Defective neutrophil oxidative burst
Impaired cytotoxic T cell function
Hypogammaglobulinemia
approach: Recurrent infection with an encapsulated bacterium points to a lack of opsonizing antibody.
In CLL the clonal B cells do not make useful antibody and they suppress normal B cells.
The result is hypogammaglobulinemia, a common cause of infection in CLL.
questions.why: CLL is a neoplasm of mature, CD5-positive, CD23-positive B cells that mostly affects older adults. The smear shows small mature lymphocytes and smudge cells, which are fragile cells crushed during smear preparation. Normal B cell function is suppressed, so most patients develop hypogammaglobulinemia. Without IgG to opsonize encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, recurrent pneumonia follows. Other features of CLL include warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia and Richter transformation to diffuse large B cell lymphoma.
whyNot: Terminal complement (C5 to C9) deficiency predisposes mainly to recurrent Neisseria infections.
A defective oxidative burst (chronic granulomatous disease) causes infections with catalase-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Aspergillus.
Impaired T cell function predisposes to viral, fungal, and intracellular infections more than to recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia.
Correct.

questions.stem: A direct antiglobulin test is positive with anti-IgG reagent and negative with anti-C3 reagent. The peripheral blood smear shows many spherocytes. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of his hemolysis?
options: IgM fixing complement in the cold, with agglutination
Warm-reacting IgG, with splenic phagocytosis
Complement lysis of cells lacking GPI-anchored proteins
Shearing of red cells on fibrin strands in small vessels
approach: A positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test means antibody or complement is on the red cell surface.
IgG without C3 that causes spherocytes is warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia, a known complication of CLL.
Splenic macrophages take bites of IgG-coated membrane, leaving spherocytes, and then remove the cells (extravascular hemolysis).
questions.why: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia is caused by IgG autoantibodies that bind red cells best at 37 °C (98.6 °F). Macrophages in the spleen bind the Fc portion of IgG and remove pieces of membrane, turning the cells into spherocytes, and then destroy them, so hemolysis is mainly extravascular. It is associated with CLL, SLE, and some drugs. Cold agglutinin disease is caused by IgM that binds in cooler body parts and fixes complement, so the direct antiglobulin test is positive for C3. It follows Mycoplasma pneumoniae or EBV infection.
whyNot: IgM cold agglutinins fix complement, so the test would be positive for C3. This is cold agglutinin disease.
Correct.
Complement lysis of cells lacking GPI-anchored CD55 and CD59 is paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, which is Coombs negative.
Shearing on fibrin strands is microangiopathic hemolysis. It produces schistocytes and a negative Coombs test.

questions.stem: His coagulation studies are normal, and no schistocytes are seen. A bone marrow biopsy shows increased numbers of megakaryocytes. Which of the following best explains his thrombocytopenia?
options: IgG against GpIIb/IIIa leading to splenic clearance
Marrow replacement of megakaryocytes by leukemic cells
Platelet consumption in widespread microvascular thrombi
Reduced hepatic synthesis of thrombopoietin
approach: Increased marrow megakaryocytes mean platelets are being made, so the problem is peripheral destruction.
Normal coagulation tests and no schistocytes argue against consumptive processes such as DIC or TTP.
Autoantibodies against platelet glycoproteins, with clearance in the spleen, are immune thrombocytopenia.
questions.why: In immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), IgG autoantibodies bind platelet membrane glycoproteins, most often GpIIb/IIIa. Splenic macrophages remove the coated platelets, and the spleen also makes much of the antibody. The marrow responds with more megakaryocytes. Platelets are low while the other lines and coagulation tests are normal, unless another process is present. Acute ITP in children follows a viral infection and usually resolves; chronic ITP in adults, mostly women, persists. ITP can also be secondary to CLL, SLE, or HIV, and ITP with autoimmune hemolysis is Evans syndrome.
whyNot: Correct.
Marrow replacement would reduce megakaryocytes. This biopsy shows them increased.
Consumption in microthrombi (DIC, TTP) causes schistocytes, and DIC prolongs clotting times. Neither is present.
Low thrombopoietin, as in liver failure, would reduce megakaryocytes rather than increase them.

questions.stem: His physician also considered another B cell neoplasm of older men that causes pancytopenia, massive splenomegaly without lymphadenopathy, and a dry tap on marrow aspiration, with cells positive for tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase and CD11c. That neoplasm is most often driven by which of the following genetic changes?
options: JAK2 V617F point mutation
BCR-ABL1 fusion from t(9;22)
BRAF V600E point mutation
Cyclin D1 overexpression from t(11;14)
approach: TRAP positivity, CD11c, massive splenomegaly, and a dry tap identify hairy cell leukemia.
Nearly all cases carry an activating BRAF V600E mutation.
BRAF V600E constantly activates the MAP kinase pathway, driving cell growth and survival.
questions.why: Hairy cell leukemia is a neoplasm of mature B cells with fine hairlike cytoplasmic projections. The cells are TRAP positive and CD11c positive. They infiltrate the splenic red pulp and the marrow, where they cause reticulin fibrosis, so aspiration often gives a dry tap. Patients have pancytopenia and massive splenomegaly, usually without lymphadenopathy, which helps separate it from CLL. Almost every case has a BRAF V600E mutation, which activates RAF-MEK-ERK signaling.
whyNot: JAK2 V617F drives myeloproliferative neoplasms such as polycythemia vera, not B cell neoplasms.
BCR-ABL1 from t(9;22) defines chronic myeloid leukemia and some cases of ALL.
Correct.
Cyclin D1 overexpression from t(11;14) defines mantle cell lymphoma, a CD5-positive B cell neoplasm.

dx: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia in a child with Down syndrome, complicated by tumor lysis syndrome
case: A 5-year-old girl with Down syndrome is brought to the physician because of fatigue, leg pain, and limping for 3 weeks. Her temperature is 38.3 °C (100.9 °F), pulse is 132/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 98/58 mm Hg. She is pale and has petechiae, tenderness over both tibias, and hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 6.9 g/dL (reference, 11.5 to 13.5 g/dL), platelets 22,000/mm3 (reference, 150,000 to 400,000/mm3), and leukocytes 86,000/mm3 (reference, 5,000 to 14,500/mm3) with 80% blasts. Bone marrow aspirate is replaced by blasts expressing CD10 and CD19. Diagnosis: precursor B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Induction chemotherapy is started.

questions.stem: Children with Down syndrome also have a greatly increased risk of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia. Which of the following findings in her blasts best identifies them as lymphoblasts?
options: Myeloperoxidase-positive cytoplasmic granules
Nuclear terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase
Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase activity
Needle-shaped cytoplasmic Auer rods
approach: Both ALL and acute megakaryoblastic leukemia occur more often in Down syndrome, so the lineage must be proven.
TdT is a DNA polymerase used in V(D)J recombination by immature B and T cells.
Nuclear TdT marks lymphoblasts; myeloperoxidase and Auer rods mark myeloid blasts.
questions.why: ALL is a neoplasm of immature lymphoid cells, mostly in children. The blasts express TdT, an enzyme that adds nucleotides during antigen receptor gene rearrangement, and B-ALL blasts also express CD10 and CD19. Children present with marrow failure (anemia, bleeding, fever) and bone pain from marrow expansion. ALL tends to spread to the CNS and testes, so CNS prophylaxis is part of treatment. Down syndrome raises the risk of both ALL and acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AML M7), so lineage markers are needed.
whyNot: Myeloperoxidase-positive granules identify myeloid blasts (AML). Lymphoblasts are myeloperoxidase negative.
Correct.
TRAP positivity marks hairy cell leukemia, a neoplasm of mature B cells in older adults.
Auer rods are fused azurophilic granules seen in myeloblasts and promyelocytes, not in lymphoblasts.

topics: Markers of lymphoid versus myeloid blasts

questions.stem: Forty-eight hours after induction begins, her urine output falls, she has muscle cramps and carpopedal spasm, and an ECG shows peaked T waves. Which of the following sets of serum findings is most likely?
options: Potassium high, phosphate high, calcium high, uric acid high
Potassium low, phosphate high, calcium low, uric acid high
Potassium high, phosphate low, calcium high, uric acid low
Potassium high, phosphate high, calcium low, uric acid high
approach: Rapid killing of a large, fast-growing leukemia releases cell contents into the blood: tumor lysis syndrome.
Cells are rich in potassium and phosphate, and their nucleic acid purines are broken down by xanthine oxidase to uric acid.
Phosphate binds calcium and precipitates, lowering serum calcium; urate and calcium phosphate crystals injure the kidney.
questions.why: Tumor lysis syndrome occurs when therapy kills a large, high-turnover tumor such as acute leukemia or Burkitt lymphoma. Released intracellular potassium causes hyperkalemia and peaked T waves. Released phosphate causes hyperphosphatemia and binds calcium, causing hypocalcemia with cramps and tetany. Purines from DNA and RNA are degraded through hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid by xanthine oxidase. Uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals deposit in renal tubules and cause acute kidney injury, which worsens the potassium and phosphate rise.
whyNot: Calcium falls in tumor lysis syndrome because released phosphate binds it. Hypercalcemia is not part of the pattern.
Potassium rises, not falls, because dying cells release their large intracellular potassium stores.
Phosphate and uric acid both rise from cell breakdown, and calcium falls.
Correct.

questions.stem: Ten days into induction her absolute neutrophil count is 300/µL (reference, 1,500 to 8,000/µL), and she develops a temperature of 38.6 °C (101.5 °F). Which of the following best describes her neutropenia?
options: Immune destruction, with mild infection risk
Splenic sequestration, with mainly viral infection risk
Marrow failure, with high bacterial and fungal risk
Inherited ELANE mutation, with infections every 21 days
approach: Classify by mechanism: her marrow is replaced by leukemia and suppressed by chemotherapy, so production has failed.
An absolute neutrophil count below 500/µL is severe neutropenia.
Severe neutropenia carries a high risk of serious bacterial and fungal infection, so this fever is treated as an emergency.
questions.why: Neutropenia can come from marrow failure (aplastic anemia, leukemia, chemotherapy), from idiosyncratic drug-induced agranulocytosis (for example with propylthiouracil), from immune destruction, or from inherited causes such as cyclic neutropenia due to ELANE mutation. Here both the leukemia and the chemotherapy shut down production. The risk of infection rises steeply as the count falls, and below 500/µL patients are at high risk of bacterial sepsis (gram-negative rods, Staphylococcus) and invasive fungal infection (Candida, Aspergillus). Fever in this setting needs immediate empiric antibiotics.
whyNot: Immune destruction is a different mechanism, and an absolute neutrophil count of 300/µL carries a high risk, not a mild one.
Splenic sequestration causes mild neutropenia, and neutropenia predisposes to bacterial and fungal infection rather than viral infection.
Correct.
Cyclic neutropenia from ELANE mutation causes recurring neutropenia about every 21 days from birth. Her neutropenia began with chemotherapy.

questions.stem: She receives a recombinant cytokine that shortens her neutropenia. Her eosinophil and monocyte counts do not change during treatment. Which of the following cytokines did she most likely receive?
options: Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor
Granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor
Interleukin-5
Thrombopoietin
approach: Match each growth factor to the lineage it drives.
G-CSF acts mainly on the neutrophil line; GM-CSF also raises monocytes and eosinophils.
A rise in neutrophils without a change in monocytes or eosinophils fits G-CSF.
questions.why: Each blood lineage has a main growth factor. Erythropoietin drives red cells, thrombopoietin drives megakaryocytes and platelets, IL-5 drives eosinophils, and G-CSF drives neutrophil production and release. GM-CSF acts earlier, on granulocyte-monocyte progenitors, so it raises neutrophils, monocytes, and eosinophils together. Recombinant G-CSF (filgrastim) is used to shorten chemotherapy-induced neutropenia.
whyNot: Correct.
GM-CSF stimulates the granulocyte-monocyte progenitor broadly, so monocytes and eosinophils would also rise.
IL-5 drives eosinophil production and would raise the eosinophil count without shortening neutropenia.
Thrombopoietin drives megakaryocytes and platelet production, not neutrophils.

dx: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis type
case: A 24-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a painless lump above her left clavicle for 2 months. She has had night sweats, generalized itching, and a 6-kg (13-lb) weight loss. Her temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg. Physical examination shows a firm, rubbery, nontender 3-cm left supraclavicular lymph node and a 2-cm left lower cervical node. Chest x-ray shows an anterior mediastinal mass. Excisional biopsy of the supraclavicular node shows broad collagen bands dividing the node into nodules containing lacunar cells, eosinophils, and small lymphocytes. The large atypical cells are positive for CD15 and CD30. Diagnosis: classical Hodgkin lymphoma, nodular sclerosis type.

questions.stem: Staging studies are performed. Which of the following features of this disease most distinguishes it from most non-Hodgkin lymphomas?
options: Frequent extranodal involvement at diagnosis
Noncontiguous spread to distant nodal groups
Orderly spread to adjacent nodal groups
Neoplastic cells forming most of the tumor mass
approach: Hodgkin lymphoma usually begins in one nodal group, often cervical or mediastinal.
It spreads in an orderly way to the next contiguous group, which is why staging guides treatment so well.
Non-Hodgkin lymphomas more often skip nodal groups and involve extranodal sites early.
questions.why: Classical Hodgkin lymphoma contains a small number of Reed-Sternberg cells and variants (CD15 and CD30 positive) in a large background of reactive cells: lymphocytes, eosinophils, histiocytes, and plasma cells. It has a bimodal age distribution, some cases are EBV associated, and nodular sclerosis is the most common type, typically in young women with a mediastinal mass. Spread is contiguous from one node group to the next, and extranodal disease is uncommon at diagnosis. Non-Hodgkin lymphomas more often spread noncontiguously and involve extranodal sites such as the gut, skin, and marrow.
whyNot: Frequent extranodal involvement is a feature of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Hodgkin lymphoma rarely starts outside lymph nodes.
Noncontiguous spread is typical of non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
Correct.
In Hodgkin lymphoma the neoplastic Reed-Sternberg cells are a small minority, often 1% to 5% of cells. Non-Hodgkin lymphomas are mostly neoplastic cells.

questions.stem: Before the biopsy, her physician considered reactive lymphadenopathy from infectious mononucleosis. A lymph node from a patient with acute Epstein-Barr virus mononucleosis would most likely show which of the following patterns?
options: Paracortical hyperplasia
Follicular hyperplasia
Sinus histiocytosis
Effacement by sheets of monotonous cells
approach: Each zone of a lymph node expands when its own cells respond: follicles (B cells), paracortex (T cells), sinuses (histiocytes).
Acute viral infection such as EBV mononucleosis produces a strong T cell response.
The T cell zone, the paracortex, expands with activated immunoblasts while node architecture is preserved.
questions.why: Reactive lymph nodes keep their normal architecture, which helps separate them from lymphoma. Follicular hyperplasia (enlarged B cell germinal centers) is seen in rheumatoid arthritis, toxoplasmosis, and early HIV infection. Paracortical hyperplasia (expanded T cell zones with immunoblasts) is seen in viral infections such as EBV, after some vaccinations, and with drugs such as phenytoin. Sinus histiocytosis is seen in nodes draining a cancer. Acute bacterial lymphangitis, as from Streptococcus pyogenes, shows red streaks tracking toward tender regional nodes.
whyNot: Correct.
Follicular hyperplasia reflects a B cell response, as in rheumatoid arthritis, toxoplasmosis, or early HIV infection.
Sinus histiocytosis is the typical reaction in nodes draining a carcinoma.
Effacement of the architecture by monotonous cells suggests non-Hodgkin lymphoma, not a reactive process.

questions.stem: Her biopsy is reviewed alongside one from a 58-year-old man with waxing and waning painless generalized lymphadenopathy for 3 years. His node is filled with closely packed neoplastic follicles of small cleaved B cells. Which of the following molecular mechanisms most likely drives his lymphoma?
options: MYC activation driving rapid cell proliferation
BCL2 overexpression blocking apoptosis
Cyclin D1 overexpression promoting the G1 to S transition
BCR-ABL1 activation causing constant kinase signaling
approach: An indolent, waxing and waning lymphoma of older adults with back-to-back follicles of small cleaved cells is follicular lymphoma.
Follicular lymphoma carries t(14;18), which places BCL2 next to the immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter.
BCL2 is antiapoptotic, so the cells accumulate instead of proliferating rapidly.
questions.why: Follicular lymphoma is an indolent B cell lymphoma with t(14;18). The translocation drives BCL2 overexpression, and BCL2 blocks the mitochondrial pathway of apoptosis, so neoplastic cells live too long. Other key non-Hodgkin lymphomas: diffuse large B cell lymphoma is the most common and is aggressive; Burkitt lymphoma has t(8;14) with MYC activation and a starry sky pattern; mantle cell lymphoma has t(11;14) with cyclin D1 overexpression and is CD5 positive; MALT lymphoma of the stomach is linked to Helicobacter pylori.
whyNot: MYC activation from t(8;14) drives Burkitt lymphoma, a highly aggressive tumor with a starry sky pattern.
Correct.
Cyclin D1 overexpression from t(11;14) drives mantle cell lymphoma.
BCR-ABL1 from t(9;22) drives chronic myeloid leukemia, not a follicular B cell lymphoma.

questions.stem: Before the biopsy, her physician also considered infectious lymphadenitis. A biopsy of a tender axillary lymph node from a different patient, a 16-year-old boy, shows stellate necrotizing granulomas with central neutrophils, and a Warthin-Starry silver stain shows clusters of small bacilli. Which of the following is the most likely organism and route of infection?
options: Streptococcus pyogenes, spread from a skin wound
Yersinia pestis, transmitted by rodent fleas
Toxoplasma gondii, from cat feces
Bartonella henselae, from a cat scratch
approach: Stellate (star-shaped) necrotizing granulomas with central neutrophils are the classic node lesion of cat scratch disease.
Small bacilli on a Warthin-Starry silver stain fit Bartonella henselae, a gram-negative bacillus carried by cats.
Plague and streptococcal infection cause suppurative nodes without granulomas, and Toxoplasma is a protozoan, not a bacillus.
questions.why: Cat scratch disease follows a scratch or bite from a cat, usually a kitten, and causes tender regional lymphadenopathy draining the inoculation site. The node shows stellate necrotizing granulomas with neutrophils in the center. Yersinia pestis, carried by rodent fleas, causes a painful, suppurative bubo and can spread to the blood (septicemic plague) and lungs (pneumonic plague); it shows bipolar safety pin staining. Streptococcus pyogenes causes acute lymphangitis with red streaks.
whyNot: Streptococcus pyogenes causes acute lymphangitis and suppurative lymphadenitis, not granulomas.
Yersinia pestis causes a painful suppurative bubo with necrosis, not stellate granulomas.
Toxoplasma is a protozoan, not a bacillus, and Toxoplasma lymphadenitis shows follicular hyperplasia with small clusters of epithelioid histiocytes, not stellate necrotizing granulomas.
Correct.

dx: Multiple myeloma with hypercalcemia and lytic bone lesions
case: A 67-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because of low back pain, fatigue, constipation, and confusion for 2 weeks. His temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 92/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 138/84 mm Hg. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL (reference, 13.5 to 17.5 g/dL), calcium 13.1 mg/dL (reference, 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL), creatinine 2.3 mg/dL (reference, 0.7 to 1.3 mg/dL), total protein 9.8 g/dL (reference, 6.0 to 8.3 g/dL), and albumin 3.4 g/dL (reference, 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). The blood smear shows rouleaux. Serum protein electrophoresis shows an IgG kappa M spike of 4.2 g/dL. Bone marrow biopsy shows 40% clonal plasma cells. X-rays show punched-out lytic lesions of the skull and lumbar spine. Diagnosis: multiple myeloma.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the main mechanism of his lytic bone lesions and hypercalcemia?
options: Tumor secretion of parathyroid hormone-related protein
Excess 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity in tumor cells
Autonomous secretion of parathyroid hormone
Osteoclast activation through increased RANKL
approach: Punched-out lesions mean focal bone resorption without new bone formation.
Myeloma cells increase RANKL on marrow stromal cells and release other osteoclast-activating factors.
Osteoclasts resorb bone and release calcium, while osteoblast activity is suppressed.
questions.why: Myeloma cells and the marrow stroma interact to raise RANKL and lower osteoprotegerin, its decoy receptor. RANKL binds RANK on osteoclast precursors, so osteoclasts multiply and resorb bone. Myeloma cells also release factors such as DKK1 that suppress osteoblasts, so the lesions are purely lytic and do not show on a bone scan. Calcium released from bone causes hypercalcemia with confusion and constipation. Other features include renal injury from light chain casts, anemia, rouleaux, infections, and an M spike.
whyNot: PTHrP causes humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy in squamous cell carcinoma and some other tumors. It is not the main mechanism in myeloma.
Excess calcitriol from 1-alpha-hydroxylase causes hypercalcemia in granulomatous disease and some lymphomas, not in myeloma.
Autonomous PTH secretion is primary hyperparathyroidism, which does not cause punched-out lesions with an M spike.
Correct.

questions.stem: Three years ago, routine testing showed an IgG kappa M protein of 1.2 g/dL with no symptoms. Which of the following findings now most clearly separates his current disease from the condition he had then?
options: IgG class of the monoclonal protein
Kappa light chain restriction of the plasma cells
End-organ damage such as lytic bone lesions
Rouleaux formation on the blood smear
approach: A small M protein without symptoms is monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS).
Both MGUS and myeloma are clonal, so the protein class and light chain restriction do not separate them.
Myeloma is defined by end-organ damage: hypercalcemia, renal injury, anemia, and bone lesions.
questions.why: MGUS is a clonal plasma cell disorder with an M protein below 3 g/dL, fewer than 10% marrow plasma cells, and no end-organ damage. It becomes myeloma at a rate of about 1% per year. Myeloma has the CRAB features: hypercalcemia, renal insufficiency, anemia, and bone lesions. Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a different disorder with an IgM M protein, hyperviscosity, and no lytic lesions. Free light chains made by plasma cell clones can also misfold and deposit as AL amyloid.
whyNot: MGUS and myeloma both most often produce IgG, so the class does not separate them.
Light chain restriction shows the cells are clonal, which is true in both MGUS and myeloma.
Correct.
Rouleaux reflect a high protein level that makes red cells stack. They can be seen with any large M protein and do not define end-organ damage.

questions.stem: His protein electrophoresis was performed on serum instead of plasma. Plasma electrophoresis could show an extra band in the beta-gamma region that might be mistaken for a small M protein. Which of the following plasma proteins causes that band?
options: Fibrinogen
Albumin
Transferrin
Haptoglobin
approach: Plasma is the fluid part of unclotted blood; serum is what remains after blood clots.
Clotting converts fibrinogen to fibrin, so serum lacks fibrinogen and consumed clotting factors.
A protein present in plasma but missing from serum must come from the clotting system.
questions.why: Plasma is about 92% water, with albumin, globulins, fibrinogen, electrolytes, nutrients, and hormones. Serum is plasma minus fibrinogen and the clotting factors used up during clotting. On electrophoresis, fibrinogen runs as a band between the beta and gamma regions and can look like a small M protein. That is why protein electrophoresis is done on serum. Albumin is the largest plasma protein and the main source of plasma oncotic pressure.
whyNot: Correct.
Albumin is present in both plasma and serum and runs as the largest band at the anodal end.
Transferrin is present in both plasma and serum. It is a normal component of the beta region.
Haptoglobin is present in both plasma and serum and runs in the alpha-2 region.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman who grew up in southern Japan has hypercalcemia, lytic bone lesions, skin nodules, and generalized lymphadenopathy. Serum protein electrophoresis shows no M spike. Her blood smear shows atypical lymphocytes with multilobed, flower-shaped nuclei. Which of the following viruses most likely caused her disease?
options: Epstein-Barr virus
Human T-lymphotropic virus type 1
Human immunodeficiency virus type 1
Human herpesvirus 8
approach: Hypercalcemia and lytic lesions without an M spike point away from myeloma.
Flower cells, skin lesions, and lymphadenopathy in a person from southern Japan or the Caribbean fit adult T cell leukemia/lymphoma.
This neoplasm of CD4-positive T cells is caused by HTLV-1.
questions.why: Adult T cell leukemia/lymphoma is a neoplasm of CD4-positive T cells caused by HTLV-1, a retrovirus endemic in southern Japan, the Caribbean, and parts of Africa and South America. Its viral Tax protein drives T cell proliferation. Patients have skin lesions, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, hypercalcemia, and lytic bone lesions, and the smear shows flower cells. Mycosis fungoides is a different T cell lymphoma of skin-homing CD4 T cells with Pautrier microabscesses; Sezary cells appear in blood when it spreads.
whyNot: EBV is linked to Burkitt lymphoma, Hodgkin lymphoma, and nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not to flower cell T cell leukemia.
Correct.
HIV raises the risk of B cell lymphomas such as diffuse large B cell lymphoma, but it does not directly transform T cells into flower cells.
HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, primary effusion lymphoma, and multicentric Castleman disease.

dx: Plasmodium falciparum malaria in a returning traveler
case: A 34-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of fever, chills, headache, and muscle aches for 3 days. He returned 12 days ago from a 3-week visit to family in Ghana and did not take malaria prophylaxis. His temperature is 39.8 °C (103.6 °F), pulse is 118/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 104/64 mm Hg. He has mild scleral icterus and a palpable spleen tip. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL (reference, 13.5 to 17.5 g/dL), platelets 62,000/mm3 (reference, 150,000 to 400,000/mm3), total bilirubin 3.0 mg/dL (reference, 0.1 to 1.2 mg/dL), mostly unconjugated, and glucose 82 mg/dL (reference, 70 to 99 mg/dL). Thin blood smear shows numerous small ring forms, several red cells with two or more rings, and crescent-shaped gametocytes, with 8% parasitemia. Diagnosis: Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

questions.stem: He asks whether the infection can come back months later, as happened to his brother after a trip to India, where Plasmodium vivax is common. Which of the following best explains why relapse is not expected with his infection?
options: P. falciparum forms no dormant hypnozoites
P. falciparum lacks a sexual gametocyte stage
P. falciparum does not pass through hepatocytes
P. falciparum infects only reticulocytes
approach: Trace the life cycle: sporozoites from the female Anopheles bite go to the liver, multiply as schizonts, and release merozoites that start the red cell cycle.
In P. vivax and P. ovale some liver forms stay dormant as hypnozoites and wake up months later, causing relapse.
P. falciparum has no hypnozoites, so once the blood stage is cleared, relapse does not occur.
questions.why: The female Anopheles mosquito injects sporozoites, which reach hepatocytes within an hour and multiply as liver schizonts (exoerythrocytic schizogony). Liver schizonts release merozoites that invade red cells and repeat asexual cycles. Some parasites become gametocytes, which a mosquito takes up to complete the sexual cycle. P. vivax and P. ovale also form hypnozoites, dormant liver stages that cause relapse and need primaquine (or tafenoquine) to eradicate. P. falciparum and P. malariae do not form hypnozoites.
whyNot: Correct.
P. falciparum does form gametocytes, the crescent-shaped forms seen on his smear.
All human Plasmodium species, including P. falciparum, go through a liver stage after the bite.
P. vivax and P. ovale prefer reticulocytes. P. falciparum invades red cells of all ages.

questions.stem: His smear shows only ring forms and gametocytes; mature trophozoites and schizonts are not seen in the peripheral blood. Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: Rupture of red cells before trophozoites can mature
Adherence of mature-stage cells to venular endothelium
Rapid clearance of mature stages by splenic macrophages
Development of mature stages only within hepatocytes
approach: As P. falciparum matures inside a red cell, it places PfEMP1 on knobs on the red cell surface.
PfEMP1 binds endothelial receptors, so cells with mature parasites stick in small venules of organs.
These sequestered cells are missing from the circulating blood, so the smear shows mostly rings.
questions.why: P. falciparum is the most dangerous species for several reasons. It invades red cells of all ages, so parasitemia can be very high. Mature parasites export PfEMP1 to knobs on the red cell membrane, and PfEMP1 binds endothelial receptors such as ICAM-1 and CD36. The cells are sequestered in small vessels of the brain, kidney, lung, and placenta, causing microvascular obstruction and avoiding removal by the spleen. The parasite switches among var genes that encode different PfEMP1 variants, so antibody responses keep falling behind.
whyNot: Rings do mature into trophozoites and schizonts. They are simply hidden in the microvasculature.
Correct.
Sequestration helps parasites avoid the spleen. Clearance does not explain the absence of mature forms.
The liver stage happens only once, before the blood stage. Red cell maturation takes place in the blood.

questions.stem: On hospital day 2, his urine becomes very dark, almost black, his urine output falls to 300 mL/24 h, and his serum creatinine rises to 3.1 mg/dL (reference, 0.7 to 1.3 mg/dL). Urine dipstick is strongly positive for blood, but microscopy shows few red cells. Which of the following most likely explains these findings?
options: Immune complex deposition in glomeruli
Obstruction of the ureters by blood clots
Ascending bacterial infection of the kidneys
Intravascular hemolysis with hemoglobinuria
approach: A dipstick positive for blood with few red cells on microscopy means free hemoglobin (or myoglobin) in the urine.
Massive rupture of parasitized red cells releases hemoglobin into the plasma, which saturates haptoglobin and is filtered.
Hemoglobin, together with sequestration in renal vessels and hypotension, injures the tubules and causes acute kidney injury.
questions.why: Severe P. falciparum malaria can cause brisk intravascular hemolysis. Free hemoglobin is filtered and makes the urine dark, a picture called blackwater fever, and acute kidney injury follows from tubular injury and microvascular sequestration. Other complications of falciparum malaria include cerebral malaria with confusion, seizures, and coma; severe anemia; hypoglycemia; and acute respiratory distress syndrome. The thin smear shows small rings, multiple rings per cell, and banana-shaped gametocytes.
whyNot: Immune complex glomerulonephritis with nephrotic syndrome is associated with chronic P. malariae infection, and it causes proteinuria rather than dark urine within days.
Ureteral clots would show red cells on microscopy and are not a feature of malaria.
Ascending pyelonephritis would show white cells and bacteria in the urine and does not cause a dipstick positive for heme without red cells.
Correct.

questions.stem: His fevers are irregular. A patient with untreated Plasmodium malariae infection, by contrast, may have fever spikes that recur every 72 hours. Each fever spike in such a patient coincides with which of the following events?
options: Release of merozoites from liver schizonts
Reactivation of hypnozoites in hepatocytes
Synchronized rupture of infected red cells
Ingestion of gametocytes by a mosquito
approach: Fever comes from host cytokines released when parasite material enters the blood.
When the erythrocytic cycles become synchronized, many schizonts rupture at the same time, releasing merozoites, pigment, and debris.
So fever spikes recur at the length of the red cell cycle: about 48 hours for P. vivax and P. ovale and 72 hours for P. malariae.
questions.why: In the erythrocytic cycle, merozoites invade red cells, mature into trophozoites and schizonts, and burst the cell to release new merozoites. When the cycles synchronize, the bursts happen together and trigger TNF and other pyrogenic cytokines, giving periodic fever. The period matches the cycle: about 48 hours (tertian) for P. vivax and P. ovale and 72 hours (quartan) for P. malariae. P. falciparum fevers are often irregular. Repeated red cell rupture also causes hemolytic anemia, and splenic work causes splenomegaly; thrombocytopenia is common.
whyNot: Merozoite release from the liver occurs once, at the start of the blood stage, so it cannot explain repeated spikes.
P. malariae does not form hypnozoites, and hypnozoite reactivation causes relapse months later, not spikes every 72 hours.
Correct.
Gametocytes taken up by a mosquito continue the cycle in the mosquito and do not cause fever in the patient.

case: A 68-year-old woman comes to the physician in July because of fever, chills, fatigue, and muscle aches for 1 week. She lives on Cape Cod, Massachusetts, and works in her garden daily. She had a splenectomy 10 years ago after a car crash. Her temperature is 39.1 °C (102.4 °F), pulse is 108/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 112/68 mm Hg. She has mild jaundice. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 8.0 g/dL (reference, 12.0 to 16.0 g/dL), reticulocytes 7% (reference, 0.5% to 2.5%), platelets 58,000/mm3 (reference, 150,000 to 400,000/mm3), LDH 820 U/L (reference, 140 to 280 U/L), haptoglobin below 10 mg/dL (reference, 30 to 200 mg/dL), and indirect bilirubin 2.8 mg/dL (reference, 0.2 to 0.8 mg/dL). The blood smear shows intraerythrocytic ring forms, some arranged in tetrads, with 9% parasitemia. Diagnosis: babesiosis.

questions.stem: Most healthy adults infected with this parasite have mild or no symptoms. Which of the following best explains the high parasitemia and severe illness in this patient?
options: Loss of complement synthesis by the spleen
Loss of splenic removal of infected red cells
Loss of splenic iron storage for erythropoiesis
Loss of splenic production of neutrophils
approach: Babesia lives inside red cells, so control depends on removing infected cells.
The spleen filters red cells and its macrophages remove infected or abnormal ones.
Without a spleen, infected cells stay in circulation and parasitemia climbs, so asplenia is a key risk factor for severe disease.
questions.why: Babesiosis is a tick-borne infection of red cells, seen mostly in the northeastern and upper midwestern United States. The spleen is the main defense: its red pulp macrophages remove parasitized red cells, and it supports antibody responses. Severe disease, with high parasitemia, hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and sometimes kidney failure or ARDS, occurs mainly in people without a spleen, older adults, and immunosuppressed patients such as those with HIV, cancer, or on rituximab.
whyNot: Most complement proteins are made by the liver, not the spleen.
Correct.
Iron for erythropoiesis is stored mainly in liver and marrow macrophages, and its loss would not raise parasitemia.
Adult neutrophils are made in the bone marrow, not the spleen.

questions.stem: Two weeks later she notices an expanding red patch with central clearing on her thigh. Which of the following organisms, transmitted by the same vector as her parasite, most likely caused this lesion?
options: Rickettsia rickettsii
Ehrlichia chaffeensis
Francisella tularensis
Borrelia burgdorferi
approach: Babesia microti is spread by the Ixodes scapularis (deer or black-legged) tick and occasionally by blood transfusion.
The same tick carries Borrelia burgdorferi, so coinfection is common in the same regions.
An expanding annular lesion with central clearing is erythema migrans of Lyme disease.
questions.why: Babesia microti is transmitted by Ixodes scapularis, the same tick that transmits Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme disease) and Anaplasma phagocytophilum. Coinfection should be considered in any patient with babesiosis. Babesia can also be transmitted by transfusion of blood from an asymptomatic donor. On smear it forms ring forms inside red cells, and the tetrad (Maltese cross) form is distinctive. Unlike malaria, there is no hemozoin pigment and no gametocytes.
whyNot: Rickettsia rickettsii causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever and is carried by Dermacentor ticks. Its rash starts on wrists and ankles.
Ehrlichia chaffeensis is carried by the lone star tick (Amblyomma) and does not cause erythema migrans.
Francisella tularensis is spread by ticks, deer flies, and contact with rabbits. It causes an ulcer with regional lymphadenopathy.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her hemolysis is partly intravascular. One week after treatment, her hemoglobin is rising and a urine dipstick is negative for blood. Which of the following urine findings at this time would best confirm that she had intravascular hemolysis?
options: Increased urobilinogen in the urine
Conjugated bilirubin detected on the urine dipstick
Hemosiderin in shed tubular epithelial cells
Red cell casts seen on urine sediment microscopy
approach: In intravascular hemolysis, free hemoglobin saturates haptoglobin, is filtered by the glomerulus, and is reabsorbed by proximal tubular cells.
Tubular cells break down the hemoglobin and store its iron as hemosiderin.
These cells are shed into the urine for weeks, so hemosiderinuria (seen with an iron stain) outlasts hemoglobinuria.
questions.why: Red cells can be destroyed inside vessels (intravascular) or by macrophages in the spleen and liver (extravascular). Both raise LDH, unconjugated bilirubin, and reticulocytes, and both can lower haptoglobin. Only intravascular hemolysis puts enough free hemoglobin into the plasma for it to be filtered by the kidney. Proximal tubular cells take up the filtered hemoglobin and store its iron as hemosiderin, and these cells are shed into the urine. Hemosiderinuria appears a few days after the hemolysis and can persist for weeks, after hemoglobinuria has cleared. On the smear, schistocytes suggest mechanical intravascular injury, while spherocytes suggest extravascular removal.
whyNot: Urobilinogen rises with any hemolysis because more bilirubin reaches the gut, and it falls back once hemolysis stops. It does not show where destruction occurred.
Hemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin, which is bound to albumin and not filtered, so the urine dipstick stays negative for bilirubin.
Correct.
Red cell casts come from bleeding into the tubules from inflamed glomeruli, as in glomerulonephritis. They are not a sign of hemolysis.

questions.stem: In a person with a normal spleen, senescent red cells are removed after about 120 days. After her splenectomy, which of the following cells took over most of this removal?
options: Hepatic Kupffer cells
Circulating neutrophils
Lymph node dendritic cells
Pulmonary alveolar macrophages
approach: Red cells lose flexibility and surface markers as they age over about 120 days.
Macrophages of the mononuclear phagocyte system recognize and engulf them, mainly in the spleen.
Without a spleen, the liver's Kupffer cells (with marrow macrophages) take over this job.
questions.why: Red cells have no nucleus and cannot repair themselves, so after about 120 days they become rigid and expose signals such as phosphatidylserine. Macrophages in the splenic red pulp remove most of them, and macrophages in the liver (Kupffer cells) and bone marrow remove the rest. After splenectomy, the liver handles most of the load, but it is less efficient at removing inclusions and parasites. That is why Howell-Jolly bodies appear on the smear and why intraerythrocytic infections such as babesiosis become severe.
whyNot: Correct.
Neutrophils phagocytose bacteria. They do not clear senescent red cells.
Dendritic cells capture and present antigen to T cells. They do not remove aged red cells.
Alveolar macrophages clear particles and microbes in the lung and are not a major site of red cell removal.

topics: Red cell life span and removal

case: A 66-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue, early satiety, and left upper abdominal fullness for 6 months. He has lost 5 kg (11 lb). His temperature is 37.2 °C (99.0 °F), pulse is 94/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 124/76 mm Hg. The spleen is palpable 14 cm below the left costal margin. Laboratory studies show hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL (reference, 13.5 to 17.5 g/dL), mean corpuscular volume 90 fL (reference, 80 to 100 fL), leukocytes 12,800/mm3 (reference, 4,500 to 11,000/mm3), and platelets 410,000/mm3 (reference, 150,000 to 400,000/mm3). The smear shows teardrop red cells, nucleated red cells, and immature granulocytes. Bone marrow aspiration yields a dry tap; biopsy shows dense reticulin and collagen fibrosis with clusters of atypical megakaryocytes. Testing shows a JAK2 V617F mutation. Diagnosis: primary myelofibrosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the marrow fibrosis in this patient?
options: Clonal proliferation of fibroblasts within the marrow
Deposition of amyloid light chains in the marrow
Growth factors released by clonal megakaryocytes
Granulomatous inflammation replacing the marrow
approach: Primary myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative neoplasm driven by JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation in a stem cell.
The neoplastic megakaryocytes release PDGF and TGF-beta.
These factors stimulate normal, nonclonal fibroblasts to lay down reticulin and collagen.
questions.why: In primary myelofibrosis the neoplastic clone includes atypical megakaryocytes that release fibrogenic growth factors such as PDGF and TGF-beta. These factors drive polyclonal (non-neoplastic) fibroblasts to fill the marrow with reticulin and collagen. The fibrotic marrow gives a dry tap. Red cells squeezed out through fibrotic marrow become teardrop cells, and immature granulocytes and nucleated red cells leak into the blood (a leukoerythroblastic picture). Hematopoiesis moves to the spleen and liver, causing massive splenomegaly.
whyNot: The fibroblasts are reactive, not part of the neoplastic clone.
Light chain amyloid deposits occur in plasma cell disorders and do not cause reticulin fibrosis with a JAK2 mutation.
Correct.
Granulomas replacing the marrow occur with tuberculosis or sarcoidosis, not with a JAK2-positive neoplasm.

questions.stem: A biopsy of the spleen would show erythroid, myeloid, and megakaryocytic precursors. The spleen can support blood cell production in this patient because it was a hematopoietic organ before birth. Which of the following sequences of hematopoietic sites during development is correct?
options: Yolk sac, then liver and spleen, then bone marrow
Bone marrow, then liver and spleen, then yolk sac
Liver and spleen, then yolk sac, then bone marrow
Yolk sac, then bone marrow, then liver and spleen
approach: Blood formation starts in yolk sac blood islands in week 3.
From about the second month, the liver becomes the main site, with help from the spleen.
The bone marrow takes over in the last months of gestation; when marrow fails after birth, liver and spleen can resume this role.
questions.why: Hematopoiesis begins in the yolk sac in the third week, moves to the liver (with a contribution from the spleen) from about the second month, and shifts to the bone marrow late in gestation. After birth, the marrow is the normal site. When the marrow is replaced by fibrosis, as in myelofibrosis, or overwhelmed by ineffective erythropoiesis, as in beta thalassemia major, the liver and spleen take up hematopoiesis again. This extramedullary hematopoiesis enlarges them, which explains his massive splenomegaly.
whyNot: Correct.
This reverses the true order. The marrow is the last site, not the first.
The yolk sac comes first, before the liver and spleen.
The liver and spleen take over before the bone marrow, not after it.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes how his JAK2 mutation promotes the growth of the neoplastic clone?
options: Fusion with BCR creates a constitutive tyrosine kinase
Loss of a tumor suppressor that blocks G1 to S transition
Overexpression of an antiapoptotic mitochondrial protein
Cytokine-independent activation of JAK-STAT signaling
approach: JAK2 is a tyrosine kinase that sits on receptors for erythropoietin, thrombopoietin, and G-CSF.
Normally it is active only when the cytokine binds.
The V617F mutation turns on the kinase without cytokine, so STAT signals for growth and survival never stop.
questions.why: JAK2 is a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase bound to type I cytokine receptors. Normally erythropoietin or thrombopoietin binding activates JAK2, which phosphorylates STAT proteins that enter the nucleus and turn on growth genes. The V617F point mutation disrupts an inhibitory region, so JAK2 signals without cytokine. It is found in nearly all polycythemia vera and in about half of essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis. In CML, by contrast, t(9;22) fuses BCR to ABL1 to make a constitutively active tyrosine kinase.
whyNot: BCR-ABL1 fusion from t(9;22) is the driver of chronic myeloid leukemia, not of JAK2-mutant neoplasms.
Loss of a G1 to S checkpoint describes tumor suppressors such as RB or p16, not JAK2.
Overexpression of the antiapoptotic protein BCL2 describes follicular lymphoma with t(14;18).
Correct.

questions.stem: His reticulocyte count is 1.0% (reference, 0.5% to 2.5%), and his red cell distribution width is increased. Which of the following best classifies his anemia?
options: Microcytic anemia from impaired heme synthesis
Normocytic anemia from marrow underproduction
Normocytic anemia from peripheral hemolysis
Macrocytic anemia from impaired DNA synthesis
approach: Classify by size: an MCV of 90 fL is normocytic.
Judge the marrow response: with hemoglobin 8.6 g/dL, a reticulocyte count of 1.0% is inappropriately low (the corrected count is well under 2%).
A low reticulocyte response means underproduction, here from marrow fibrosis.
questions.why: Anemia is classified first by MCV: below 80 fL is microcytic, 80 to 100 fL is normocytic, and above 100 fL is macrocytic. Next comes the reticulocyte count, which shows whether the marrow is responding. Correcting for anemia (1.0% times 8.6 divided by a normal hemoglobin of about 15 g/dL) gives about 0.6%, far too low for this degree of anemia, so production is inadequate. In hemolysis the reticulocyte count would be high. The raised RDW reflects the mix of teardrop cells and other abnormal shapes.
whyNot: His MCV is 90 fL, which is normocytic, not microcytic. Impaired heme synthesis (iron deficiency) gives a low MCV.
Correct.
Hemolysis causes a high reticulocyte count. His count is inappropriately low.
His MCV is normal. Impaired DNA synthesis (B12 or folate deficiency) gives an MCV above 100 fL.

dx: Severe dengue with plasma leakage and thrombocytopenia
case: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, and bleeding gums. She returned from Thailand 6 days ago. She had high fever, headache, eye pain, and muscle aches for 4 days, and the fever resolved yesterday. She had dengue during a trip to Brazil 3 years ago. Her temperature is 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), pulse is 122/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 92/76 mm Hg. She has petechiae, a tender enlarged liver, shifting dullness, and decreased breath sounds at the right lung base. Laboratory studies show hematocrit 50% (reference, 36% to 46%), up from 38% 2 days ago, platelets 24,000/mm3 (reference, 150,000 to 400,000/mm3), and albumin 2.6 g/dL (reference, 3.5 to 5.5 g/dL). Dengue NS1 antigen is positive. Diagnosis: severe dengue with plasma leakage.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why her current illness is more severe than her first dengue infection?
options: Antibody-dependent enhancement by heterotypic antibodies
Reactivation of latent virus from the first infection
Loss of immunity to the serotype of the first infection
Coinfection with chikungunya virus from the same mosquito
approach: There are four dengue virus serotypes; infection gives lasting immunity only to the same serotype.
On reinfection with a different serotype, old antibodies bind the new virus without neutralizing it.
The antibody-coated virus enters Fc receptor-bearing monocytes and macrophages more easily, raising viral load and cytokine release that make capillaries leak.
questions.why: Dengue is a flavivirus spread by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. A second infection with a different serotype is the main risk factor for severe dengue. Cross-reactive, non-neutralizing antibodies from the first infection help the new virus enter monocytes through Fc receptors (antibody-dependent enhancement). The result is higher viremia, strong cytokine release, plasma leakage, and severe thrombocytopenia, often starting as the fever ends. The same Aedes mosquitoes spread chikungunya, known for long-lasting arthralgia, and Zika, known for congenital microcephaly.
whyNot: Correct.
Dengue virus does not establish latency, so it cannot reactivate.
Immunity to the first serotype is long lasting. Severe disease follows infection with a different serotype.
Chikungunya is spread by the same mosquitoes, but it causes fever with severe, persistent arthralgia, not plasma leakage. Her NS1 test confirms dengue.

questions.stem: Her serum albumin is 2.6 g/dL. Which change in the Starling forces across her capillaries results most directly from this finding?
options: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure
Decreased capillary oncotic pressure
Increased interstitial hydrostatic pressure
Decreased lymphatic flow from the interstitium
approach: Albumin supplies most of the oncotic pressure of plasma.
Low albumin lowers capillary oncotic pressure, which normally pulls fluid back into vessels.
Net filtration rises and fluid collects in the interstitium and body cavities, adding to the leak from damaged capillaries.
questions.why: Starling forces set fluid movement across capillaries: capillary hydrostatic pressure and interstitial oncotic pressure push fluid out, while capillary oncotic pressure and interstitial hydrostatic pressure pull it in. Albumin is the main contributor to plasma oncotic pressure, so hypoalbuminemia favors edema, ascites, and effusions. In severe dengue, leaky capillaries also let albumin escape, which lowers serum albumin further. Albumin also carries unconjugated bilirubin, fatty acids, and much of the plasma calcium, so a low albumin lowers the measured total calcium.
whyNot: Increased hydrostatic pressure causes edema in heart failure or venous obstruction, not from low albumin.
Correct.
Interstitial hydrostatic pressure rises as fluid accumulates, which opposes filtration. It is a consequence, not the direct effect of low albumin.
Lymphatic obstruction causes protein-rich lymphedema and is unrelated to serum albumin.

questions.stem: On hospital day 2 she oozes blood from venipuncture sites, and her serum creatinine rises to 2.4 mg/dL (reference, 0.6 to 1.1 mg/dL). Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time are prolonged, fibrinogen is 90 mg/dL (reference, 200 to 400 mg/dL), D-dimer is markedly increased, and the smear shows schistocytes. Which of the following best explains both her bleeding and her kidney injury?
options: Autoantibodies against platelet glycoproteins
Inherited deficiency of factor VIII
Microthrombi consuming factors and platelets
Reduced hepatic synthesis of clotting factors
approach: Prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, low platelets, and schistocytes together mean disseminated intravascular coagulation.
Widespread activation of coagulation forms fibrin microthrombi in small vessels, which injure organs such as the kidney.
The same process uses up platelets and clotting factors, and fibrinolysis is activated, so the patient bleeds from puncture sites and mucosa.
questions.why: DIC is always secondary, here to severe viral infection with endothelial injury and shock. Tissue factor and cytokines trigger coagulation throughout the circulation. Fibrin microthrombi block small vessels in the kidney, lungs, brain, and adrenals, causing ischemic injury, and red cells sheared on fibrin strands become schistocytes. At the same time, platelets, fibrinogen, and other factors are consumed, and plasmin breaks down fibrin (raising D-dimer), so the patient bleeds. Clotting and bleeding happen together.
whyNot: Antiplatelet autoantibodies cause immune thrombocytopenia, with normal PT, aPTT, and fibrinogen and no schistocytes.
Hemophilia A prolongs only the aPTT, presents with joint and muscle bleeding from childhood, and does not cause microthrombi.
Correct.
Liver dysfunction prolongs PT and aPTT, but it does not explain the high D-dimer, schistocytes, and kidney injury from microthrombi.

questions.stem: Her physician also considered other viral hemorrhagic fevers. A nurse who cared for patients during an outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo develops fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and bleeding, and a filamentous RNA virus is isolated. How was this nurse most likely infected?
options: Bite of an infected Aedes mosquito
Inhalation of aerosolized rodent excreta
Bite of an infected Ixodes tick
Direct contact with infected body fluids
approach: A filamentous RNA virus causing hemorrhagic fever in central Africa is a filovirus: Ebola or Marburg.
Filoviruses spread from person to person through direct contact with blood and other body fluids of sick patients.
Health care workers and family caregivers are at high risk; fruit bats are the likely natural reservoir.
questions.why: Ebola and Marburg viruses are filoviruses, long filamentous RNA viruses. Fruit bats are the likely reservoir, and outbreaks begin when a person is infected by contact with an animal. The virus then spreads between people through direct contact with blood, vomit, stool, and other body fluids, so caregivers are at high risk. Illness starts with fever and progresses to vomiting, diarrhea, hemorrhage, DIC, and multiorgan failure. Dengue, by contrast, is spread by Aedes mosquitoes and not from person to person.
whyNot: Aedes mosquitoes spread dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever, not filoviruses.
Inhaled rodent excreta spread hantavirus, a bunyavirus that causes pulmonary syndrome or hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome.
Ixodes ticks transmit Babesia, Borrelia, and Anaplasma, not filoviruses.
Correct.
